section_title: What does it mean to welcome Onesimus as a brother?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 8 So although in Christ I am bold enough to order you to do what is proper, 9 I prefer to appeal on the basis of love. For I, Paul, am now aged, and a prisoner of Christ Jesus as well. 10 I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whose father I became while I was in chains. 11 Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me.

12 I am sending back to you him who is my very heart. 13 I would have liked to keep him with me, so that on your behalf he could minister to me in my chains for the gospel. 14 But I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will. 15 For perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while, so that you might have him back for good— 16 no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother. He is especially beloved to me, but even more so to you, both in person and in the Lord.

17 So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me. 18 But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account. 19 I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me your very self. 20 Yes, brother, let me have some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ.

21 Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask. 22 In the meantime, prepare a guest room for me, because I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you.

context_lines: Paul moves from thanking Philemon for his love to asking him to show that love toward Onesimus. He could issue a command, but chooses an appeal. He wants Philemon’s response to be willing rather than forced.

Onesimus has become Paul’s child in the faith during his imprisonment. The word translated [child](https://biblehub.com/greek/5043.htm) can describe the relationship between a teacher and a disciple. Paul is speaking about coming to faith through his ministry, not a physical birth. Onesimus’s name means useful or beneficial, and Paul plays on that name: the man formerly described as useless has become useful to them both.

Paul is sending him back, although he would gladly have kept him nearby to help. His request changes the terms of the welcome: Philemon is to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother, and to welcome him as he would Paul himself. Paul suggests that their separation may have led to a lasting good. His word perhaps matters; he does not claim to know every reason God allowed it.

If Onesimus has caused a loss or owes anything, Paul offers to pay. The verb translated [charge it to my account](https://biblehub.com/greek/1677.htm) means to put a charge against someone’s account. Paul makes that offer personally, in his own handwriting. The sentence is conditional; it does not tell us exactly what Onesimus did or how much he owed.

Paul expects a generous response and asks for a guest room, hoping to be restored to them through their prayers. The letter gives the appeal and the hope, but does not report Philemon’s answer or Paul’s eventual visit.
common_interpretation_lines: [Calvin](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/philemon/1.htm) and [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-philemon/) both emphasize Paul’s affectionate appeal, the change in Onesimus and the welcome now owed to him as a fellow believer. Both understand Paul’s offer to pay as removing an obstacle to that welcome. The appeal asks Philemon to act on the faith and love Paul has already commended.

The question of legal freedom needs care. Calvin reads the letter as requiring a forgiving reception without removing the master’s existing civil authority. Wesley’s introduction suggests that Philemon may actually have freed Onesimus, although his note on verse 16 still describes service alongside Christian brotherhood. These are named teachers’ readings, not a complete statement of every Reformed or Wesleyan view. Paul explicitly requires the welcome of a beloved brother; the letter does not record a formal release or its outcome.

Calvin also reads the request for lodging as a real hope of release, subject to God’s will, rather than a guarantee. Wesley likewise understands verse 22 as restoration to liberty. Their readings allow the prayer to concern Paul’s actual circumstances without promising that every requested outcome will occur.
god_plan_lines: [Galatians 3:26–29](https://biblehub.com/bsb/galatians/3.htm) says that those who belong to Christ share the standing of God’s children, including slave and free. [Colossians 3:11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/colossians/3.htm) likewise places both within the new life in Christ. Philemon shows what that shared belonging asks of a particular relationship: the person being sent back is to be welcomed as a brother.

Paul’s offer to bear a cost so Onesimus can be received provides a limited parallel to the reconciliation described in [2 Corinthians 5:18–21](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_corinthians/5.htm). There God reconciles people to Himself through Christ and entrusts a message of reconciliation to His servants. Paul is helping two people be reconciled; his promise to pay a possible debt is not another sacrifice for sin.

There is also a parallel with Joseph’s story in [Genesis 50:15–21](https://biblehub.com/bsb/genesis/50.htm): God can bring good through events which caused real harm. Joseph states what God accomplished in his story. Paul speaks more cautiously about Onesimus’s separation. Neither passage turns the harm itself into something good or promises that every loss will soon have an explanation.
